assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks with neutral atoms at the 10^-18 level are a decisive advance in precision measurement. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the lattice light shift while retaining the statistics of many atoms in parallel, and Ye's implementation brought stability and accuracy to a new regime. This is atomic physics at its most elegant: control of internal and motional states, together with an understanding of systematic shifts such as blackbody radiation, polarisability and collisions, enables tests of relativity, searches for varying constants and relativistic geodesy, and prepares a redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated early strontium lattice clocks; Ye's group drove the strontium clock to record accuracy and stability and developed the spatially resolved many-body clock. The two-name list is a clean, fair prize configuration. Earlier prizes recognised the frequency comb (Hall, Hansch) and ion clocks (Wineland), so the new contribution is distinct, but the credit of other leading groups (for example Lemonde, Bloom, Ludlow, Schmidt, Hinkley) is not carried in the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmations across several continents, with multiple species (Sr, Yb, Hg), clock comparisons well below 10^-18 and formal progress toward a redefinition of the second. Recognition is timely and the interpretation is stable.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize for ion-based control and with the 2005 comb prize may be argued by some, although the lattice-clock step is distinct.
Which of the several competing lattice-clock groups deserve credit beyond the two supplied names is not settled by the evidence I have; I have not verified specific priority claims independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Realising strongly correlated lattice models with ultracold atoms, such as the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition and the Fermi-Hubbard model, opened quantum simulation as an experimental discipline, with single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopes as a further step. It rests on trapping, cooling and probing methods that the atomic physics community has developed over decades, and has become a central platform for many-body physics. The work is original, conceptually clear and lasting, and it links atomic and condensed matter physics.
assessment.attribution: The theoretical proposal (Jaksch, Zoller, Cirac and collaborators) and the experiments (Greiner and Bloch for the Mott transition, Esslinger for fermionic lattices and Hubbard physics, and Bloch and Greiner for microscopes) form a layered credit. Five names are supplied and at most three can be chosen; I propose the experimental leaders, which leaves the theoretical origin partly unrecognised, and I would see Zoller and Cirac as an alternative theory-weighted configuration.
assessment.maturity: The foundational demonstrations date from around 2002 and have been replicated widely; analogue simulation of Fermi-Hubbard physics at low temperature is still progressing, so the strongest scientific payoff may lie ahead, but the core discovery is well established.
uncertainties: The theory-versus-experiment balance and the possible overlap with a trapped-ion or Rydberg-array prize make the three-person configuration contestable.
Whether the full Fermi-Hubbard programme has reached the maturity of the Mott-insulator result is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapped ions combine the original Cirac-Zoller gate proposal with experiments showing high-fidelity multi-qubit gates, entanglement and digital and analogue quantum simulation. The platform is among the leading architectures for quantum computing, and its precision builds on atomic and ion-trap techniques that I know well. The scientific significance is high.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the ion-trap quantum computer in 1995; Blatt led a major experimental programme with entanglement, teleportation and quantum simulation. Wineland and the NIST group (and groups at Innsbruck, Oxford and Maryland) carried out foundational gate demonstrations. The 2012 prize to Wineland already covered measurement and manipulation of single quantum systems, which creates a partial overlap and a sensitive credit question.
assessment.maturity: Confirmation is strong and independent across many groups and companies, with the technique mature, although scalable fault-tolerant computing remains a goal and not a result.
uncertainties: The 2012 Wineland-Haroche prize may be seen as having already recognised much of the experimental foundation.
The credit between the NIST, Innsbruck and other groups for gate demonstrations is not resolved by the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall and quantum anomalous Hall effects form a landmark of modern condensed matter physics: the Kane-Mele and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang predictions, the HgTe experiment and the zero-field quantised Hall conductance. The concepts are original and have been highly influential across physics, although this is outside my own field and I assess it more from general knowledge.
assessment.attribution: Kane (theory), Molenkamp (experimental quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe) and Xue (quantum anomalous Hall) cover distinct components of a compound discovery. Credit for the theory is shared with Mele, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (the last deceased), and the supplied list does not include several of these, so the allocation is unsettled.
assessment.maturity: Experimental confirmation has been strong for quantum spin Hall transport in HgTe and the quantum anomalous Hall effect, and the field is mature, but the high-temperature promise has not yet fully materialised in applications.
uncertainties: The decisive credit for the theoretical prediction is contested and the proposed three-name group omits several candidates.
The compound candidate bundles quantum spin Hall and quantum anomalous Hall results that may need different recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Strongly interacting Fermi gases and the BEC-BCS crossover tuned through Feshbach resonances turned ultracold atoms into an experimentally controlled testbed for strongly correlated fermions, with the observation of vortices, condensates of molecules and universality at unitarity. It is clean physics with relevance to superconductors and neutron matter, and a natural continuation of the 2001 condensation prize.
assessment.attribution: Grimm and Salomon (and Jin and Ketterle's groups) produced molecular condensates and studied the crossover; Thomas observed strongly interacting behaviour at unitarity. Deborah Jin, who led key early experiments, has died, and Ketterle already holds a prize, which complicates a fair three-person configuration based on the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: The results are well confirmed by independent groups over two decades, and the interpretation is stable. Recognition is not premature, and the field is mature.
uncertainties: Absence of Jin from any living configuration and the roles of Ketterle and Zwierlein make the credit picture incomplete.
Precisely how the order of priority between the 2003-2004 experimental groups should be assigned is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Pulsar timing arrays have reported evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background, opening a new window on supermassive black-hole binaries or exotic physics. If confirmed it would be a major discovery, and I admire the long-term, precision-timing character of the work.
assessment.attribution: The credit is spread over several collaborations (NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA, CPTA, IPTA), and the three supplied names reflect founding or leadership roles more than a single decisive discovery; a three-person configuration would be difficult to justify as a fair summary of a very large collective effort.
assessment.maturity: The 2023 evidence is at the level of a few sigma in individual arrays with a Hellings-Downs signature; the source of the signal is not yet established. Recognition may be somewhat premature, and I would wait for stronger combined detections.
uncertainties: Detection significance and astrophysical versus cosmological origin are unsettled.
Attribution among large collaborations is difficult and the supplied names may not capture the decisive contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics, with superconducting artificial atoms coupled strongly to microwave resonators, is the basis of a leading quantum-computing architecture and provides precise control and readout of quantum states in an engineered system. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, so there is a thematic link, but circuit QED is a distinct and broad advance.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 theory and the Yale experiments, and Wallraff's strong-coupling demonstration was reported in the same year. Four names are supplied and three can be proposed; excluding Girvin is a real cost, and it is unclear whether the 2025 laureates' work makes a further prize in this area appropriate soon.
assessment.maturity: The result is replicated and widely used, with transmon qubits and quantum error correction demonstrations underlying a large industry. The maturity is high, although timing so soon after the 2025 prize may feel crowded.
uncertainties: Closeness to the 2025 prize may delay recognition of circuit QED.
The split between theory (Blais, Girvin) and experiment (Schoelkopf, Wallraff) cannot be settled from the supplied text, and the transmon invention itself is not named in the candidate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry underlies precision measurements of gravity, rotation and fundamental constants, as well as tests of the equivalence principle and gravitational-wave proposals. It makes direct use of laser cooling and matter-wave coherence and is an area where I have good background judgement. Its impact is solid and lasting, although it has not produced a single defining discovery.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard (early atom interferometer with gratings), Kasevich and Chu (light-pulse interferometry), Bordé (theory of the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer) and Schmiedmayer (chip and coherent manipulation) all have claims, and Chu already has a prize partly connected to atom cooling. Any three-name selection is arguable.
assessment.maturity: The techniques are mature and in use in metrology, but the grand fundamental-physics goals remain future work, so the discovery component is less sharp.
uncertainties: Priority among Pritchard, Kasevich, Bordé and others is contested.
It is unclear whether a prize would be tied to a specific discovery or to a general technique.
